title: Θεῶν ἔρις
titleEn: The Gods Go to War — Iliad 20.1–102
about: Both armies arm on the plain, and Zeus sends Themis to call every god, river and nymph to the assembly on Olympus. Poseidon asks why; Zeus says he will stay and watch while the others go down and help whichever side they like, because Achilles alone might sack the wall even beyond fate. The gods split in two: Hera, Athena, Poseidon, Hermes and Hephaestus go to the Achaeans; Ares, Apollo, Artemis, Leto, Xanthus and Aphrodite to the Trojans. While they hold back the Achaeans exult and the Trojans tremble at the sight of Achilles. When the gods join the fighting, Strife rises, Zeus thunders, Poseidon shakes the earth, and Aidoneus leaps from his throne for fear his dank house will be laid open. The gods stand matched pair by pair. Achilles longs to meet Hector, but Apollo, in the voice of Lycaon, rouses Aeneas against him. Aeneas answers that he has already fled Achilles once and was saved by Zeus, that no man can fight him, and that a god is always at his side.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἳ μὲν παρὰ νηυσὶ κορωνίσι θωρήσσοντο
ἀμφὶ σὲ Πηλέος υἱὲ μάχης ἀκόρητον Ἀχαιοί,
Τρῶες δ’ αὖθ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἐπὶ θρωσμῷ πεδίοιο·
sentences.i: So the Achaeans were arming themselves by the curved ships around you, son of Peleus, who cannot have enough of battle, while on the other side the Trojans were drawn up on the rising ground of the plain;
sentences.n: The ‘they’ of ὣς οἳ μέν are the Achaeans, who are named only at the end of line 2. The poet turns and speaks straight to Achilles, σὲ Πηλέος υἱέ ‘you, son of Peleus’, without naming him; ἀκόρητον is accusative agreeing with σέ, and μάχης is the genitive it governs, ‘insatiate of battle’. θωρήσσοντο is the imperfect middle of θωρήσσω ‘arm’. κορωνίσι ‘curved’ is the stock epithet of ships. θρωσμῷ is a swell of ground, ‘rising ground’, and ἑτέρωθεν ‘from the other side’ puts the Trojans opposite.

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς δὲ Θέμιστα κέλευσε θεοὺς ἀγορὴν δὲ καλέσσαι
κρατὸς ἀπ’ Οὐλύμποιο πολυπτύχου·
sentences.l:
And Zeus Themis commanded the gods to assembly to call
from the head of Olympus, many-folded;
sentences.i: Zeus ordered Themis to call the gods to assembly from the crest of many-folded Olympus;
sentences.n: Θέμιστα is accusative, the object of κέλευσε, with the infinitive καλέσσαι (aorist of καλέω, with the doubled σ); her name is also the word θέμις ‘what is right, custom’. ἀγορὴν δέ is ἀγορήν ‘to assembly’ with the suffix -δε of direction, as with πόλεμον δέ in line 32. κρατὸς ἀπ’ is ‘from the head’, that is, the summit, and Οὐλύμποιο has the epic genitive -οιο. πολυπτύχου ‘many-folded’ is from πτύξ ‘fold’, the folds of a mountain.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἄρα πάντῃ
φοιτήσασα κέλευσε Διὸς πρὸς δῶμα νέεσθαι.
sentences.l:
and she, then, in every direction
having gone about, commanded them to the house of Zeus to go.
sentences.i: She went about in every direction and told them to go to the house of Zeus.
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ ‘and she’ is Themis, the article used as a pronoun. φοιτήσασα is the aorist participle of φοιτάω ‘go to and fro’, and πάντῃ ‘in every direction’. κέλευσε takes the infinitive νέεσθαι, the uncontracted form of νέομαι ‘go, come’; πρὸς δῶμα ‘to the house’.

sentences.t:
οὔτέ τις οὖν ποταμῶν ἀπέην νόσφ’ Ὠκεανοῖο,
οὔτ’ ἄρα νυμφάων αἵ τ’ ἄλσεα καλὰ νέμονται
καὶ πηγὰς ποταμῶν καὶ πίσεα ποιήεντα.
sentences.l:
So not one of the rivers was absent, apart from Oceanus,
nor, then, of the nymphs, who inhabit the fair groves
and the springs of rivers and the grassy meadows.
sentences.i: Not one of the rivers was missing except Oceanus, nor any of the nymphs who dwell in the fair groves, the springs of rivers, and grassy water-meadows.
sentences.n: ἀπέην is the imperfect of ἄπειμι ‘be away’ in its epic form (Attic ἀπῆν), and νόσφ’ is νόσφι ‘apart from’ with the genitive, so only Oceanus stays away. οὔτέ … οὔτ’ is ‘not … nor’. The nymphs are named by where they live: ἄλσεα ‘groves’, πηγάς ‘springs’ and πίσεα ‘water-meadows’, with νέμονται ‘inhabit’ governing all three. Line 9 is a line the Odyssey also has, and its English is the Odyssey’s.

sentences.t:
ἐλθόντες δ’ ἐς δῶμα Διὸς νεφεληγερέταο
ξεστῇς αἰθούσῃσιν ἐνίζανον, ἃς Διὶ πατρὶ
Ἥφαιστος ποίησεν ἰδυίῃσι πραπίδεσσιν.
sentences.l:
And having come to the house of cloud-gatherer Zeus
in the polished colonnades they sat, which for Zeus the father
Hephaestus made with knowing wits.
sentences.i: They came to the house of Zeus who gathers the clouds and sat down in the polished colonnades that Hephaestus had made for father Zeus with his skilled wits.
sentences.n: ἐλθόντες is the aorist participle ‘having come’, and ἐνίζανον the imperfect of ἐνιζάνω ‘sat down in’. ξεστῇς αἰθούσῃσιν is a dative plural, ‘in polished colonnades’ (ξεστός ‘smoothed’; an αἴθουσα is the roofed portico in front of a hall). ἃς is the relative ‘which’, with Ἥφαιστος the subject of ποίησεν. ἰδυίῃσι πραπίδεσσιν ‘with knowing wits’: ἰδυίῃσι is the dative plural feminine of the perfect participle ἰδυῖα ‘knowing’, and πραπίδες are the ‘wits’. νεφεληγερέταο is the genitive of the stock epithet ‘cloud-gatherer’.

sentences.t: ὣς οἳ μὲν Διὸς ἔνδον ἀγηγέρατ’·
sentences.l: So they within the house of Zeus were gathered;
sentences.i: So they were gathered inside the house of Zeus;
sentences.n: ἀγηγέρατ’ is the third plural pluperfect passive of ἀγείρω ‘gather’ (ἀγηγέρατο, the last vowel elided), ‘were gathered’. Διὸς ἔνδον is ‘within (the house) of Zeus’. ὣς οἳ μέν ‘so they’ sums up the arrival and sets up the late guest in the next line.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἐνοσίχθων
νηκούστησε θεᾶς, ἀλλ’ ἐξ ἁλὸς ἦλθε μετ’ αὐτούς,
ἷζε δ’ ἄρ’ ἐν μέσσοισι, Διὸς δ’ ἐξείρετο βουλήν·
sentences.l:
and not the earth-shaker
was deaf to the goddess, but out of the sea came among them,
and sat in the midst, and of Zeus questioned the plan:
sentences.i: and the earth-shaker did not turn a deaf ear to the goddess either, but came out of the sea among them, sat down in the middle, and questioned Zeus about his plan:
sentences.n: ἐνοσίχθων ‘earth-shaker’ is Poseidon (the poem names him at line 34); the epithet stands in for the name. νηκούστησε is νη- ‘not’ + ἀκούω ‘hear’, to be deaf to a summons, and θεᾶς is the genitive after it: Themis, who has been sent round. ἐξ ἁλός ‘out of the sea’ (ἅλς, genitive ἁλός). ἷζε is the unaugmented imperfect of ἵζω ‘sit’, and ἐν μέσσοισι ‘in the middle of them’. ἐξείρετο is the imperfect middle of ἐξείρομαι ‘question’, with Διὸς βουλήν ‘the plan of Zeus’ as its object.

sentences.t: τίπτ’ αὖτ’ ἀργικέραυνε θεοὺς ἀγορὴν δὲ κάλεσσας;
sentences.l: “Why again, you of the bright thunderbolt, have you called the gods to assembly?
sentences.i: “Why have you called the gods to assembly again, you of the bright thunderbolt?
sentences.n: Poseidon speaks. τίπτ’ is τίπτε ‘why’ (τί ποτε, the ποτέ giving ‘why on earth’), here with its last vowel elided; αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘again, in turn’. ἀργικέραυνε is a vocative, ‘of the bright thunderbolt’ (ἀργής ‘bright’ + κεραυνός ‘thunderbolt’), a stock epithet of Zeus. θεοὺς ἀγορὴν δὲ κάλεσσας repeats the words of line 4, with κάλεσσας the aorist of καλέω.

sentences.t: ἦ τι περὶ Τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν μερμηρίζεις;
sentences.l: Are you, perhaps, in doubt about something concerning the Trojans and the Achaeans?
sentences.i: Are you in doubt between two courses about something that concerns the Trojans and the Achaeans?
sentences.n: ἦ opens a question (‘is it that …?’), and τι is ‘something’. μερμηρίζεις is the second singular of μερμηρίζω ‘be in doubt between two courses’, the verb for a mind weighing what to do; Poseidon is guessing what is on Zeus’s mind. περὶ Τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν ‘about the Trojans and the Achaeans’.

sentences.t: τῶν γὰρ νῦν ἄγχιστα μάχη πόλεμός τε δέδηε.
sentences.l: For of them now nearest battle and war is blazing.”
sentences.i: For the battle and the war are blazing very close to them now.”
sentences.n: τῶν ‘of them’ is the Trojans and Achaeans, the genitive that goes with ἄγχιστα ‘nearest’, so the fighting is blazing right beside them. δέδηε is the perfect of δαίω ‘burn’ with present force, ‘is blazing’; the singular verb serves μάχη and πόλεμος as one pair. Poseidon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: In answer Zeus who gathers the clouds said to him:
sentences.n: This is the formula that opens a reply. τόν ‘him’ is Poseidon, the article used as a pronoun; ἀπαμειβόμενος is ‘answering’ and προσέφη ‘addressed’. νεφεληγερέτα is the nominative of the stock epithet with the epic -α for -ης, translated every time. The line is the same as one in the Odyssey and has that unit’s English.

sentences.t:
ἔγνως ἐννοσίγαιε ἐμὴν ἐν στήθεσι βουλὴν
ὧν ἕνεκα ξυνάγειρα·
sentences.l:
“You have understood, earth-shaker, the plan in my breast,
for the sake of which I gathered you together;
sentences.i: “You have understood, earth-shaker, the plan in my breast, the reason I gathered you together;
sentences.n: Zeus answers. ἔγνως is the aorist of γιγνώσκω ‘come to know’, ‘you have understood’. ἐννοσίγαιε is the vocative of ἐννοσίγαιος ‘earth-shaker’, a second epithet of Poseidon, built on γαῖα ‘earth’ where ἐνοσίχθων uses χθών. ἐμὴν ἐν στήθεσι βουλήν ‘my plan in my breast’. ὧν ἕνεκα is ‘for the sake of which’ (the relative is plural, ‘for which things’), and ξυνάγειρα is the aorist of συναγείρω ‘gather together’.

sentences.t: μέλουσί μοι ὀλλύμενοί περ.
sentences.l: they are a care to me, perishing though they are.
sentences.i: They matter to me, even though they are dying.
sentences.n: μέλουσι is the third plural of μέλω ‘be a care to’, with μοι ‘to me’. ‘They’ are the men on the plain, not yet named. ὀλλύμενοι is the present participle of ὄλλυμι ‘destroy; (middle) perish’, and περ gives it the force ‘even though’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤτοι μὲν ἐγὼ μενέω πτυχὶ Οὐλύμποιο
ἥμενος, ἔνθ’ ὁρόων φρένα τέρψομαι·
sentences.l:
But I indeed will stay in a fold of Olympus,
sitting, there, looking on I shall delight my mind;
sentences.i: But I shall stay in a fold of Olympus, sitting there, and looking on I shall delight my mind;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι μὲν ἐγώ sets Zeus against οἳ δὲ δὴ ἄλλοι ‘the rest of you’ in the next line. μενέω is the uncontracted future of μένω ‘stay’, and πτυχί the dative of πτύξ ‘fold’, here a fold of the mountain. ἥμενος ‘sitting’; ἔνθ’ ‘there’; ὁρόων is the uncontracted participle ‘looking on’. φρένα τέρψομαι ‘I shall delight my mind’, with φρένα an accusative of respect.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ δὴ ἄλλοι
ἔρχεσθ’ ὄφρ’ ἂν ἵκησθε μετὰ Τρῶας καὶ Ἀχαιούς,
ἀμφοτέροισι δ’ ἀρήγεθ’ ὅπῃ νόος ἐστὶν ἑκάστου.
sentences.l:
but you others, then,
go until you come among the Trojans and the Achaeans,
and help both sides in whatever way each one’s mind is set.
sentences.i: but the rest of you, go until you reach the Trojans and the Achaeans, and give help to both sides as each of you is minded.
sentences.n: οἳ δὲ δὴ ἄλλοι is ‘but you others, then’: the other gods, addressed directly. ἔρχεσθ’ is the imperative ἔρχεσθε ‘go’; ὄφρ’ ἂν ἵκησθε ‘until you come’ is ὄφρα ἄν with the aorist subjunctive of ἱκνέομαι. ἀμφοτέροισι ‘to both sides’; ἀρήγεθ’ is the imperative ἀρήγετε ‘help’. ὅπῃ νόος ἐστὶν ἑκάστου ‘in whatever way the mind of each is set’ leaves the choice of side to each god.

sentences.t:
εἰ γὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς οἶος ἐπὶ Τρώεσσι μαχεῖται
οὐδὲ μίνυνθ’ ἕξουσι ποδώκεα Πηλεΐωνα.
sentences.l:
For if Achilles alone against the Trojans will fight,
not even a little while will they hold off fleet-footed the son of Peleus.
sentences.i: For if Achilles fights alone against the Trojans, they will not hold off the fleet-footed son of Peleus even for a little while.
sentences.n: Zeus gives the reason. εἰ … μαχεῖται is ‘if he will fight’ (εἰ with the future), and οἶος is ‘alone’. ἕξουσι is the future of ἔχω, here ‘hold off, hold back’, with οὐδὲ μίνυνθ’ ‘not even for a little while’ (μίνυνθα). ποδώκεα Πηλεΐωνα is accusative: ποδώκης ‘fleet-footed’ is a stock epithet and Πηλεΐων ‘son of Peleus’ a patronymic, both translated every time.

sentences.t: καὶ δέ τί μιν καὶ πρόσθεν ὑποτρομέεσκον ὁρῶντες·
sentences.l: And even before, in some measure, they used to tremble before him, looking at him;
sentences.i: Even before this they used to tremble a little at the sight of him;
sentences.n: καὶ δέ τί μιν is ‘and even, somewhat, him’, with πρόσθεν ‘before’. ὑποτρομέεσκον is the iterative imperfect of ὑποτρομέω ‘tremble’: the suffix -εσκ- means ‘used to’, and ὑπο- here has the sense of ‘a little’. ὁρῶντες ‘looking at (him)’. The ‘they’ are the Trojans, left unnamed.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ὅτε δὴ καὶ θυμὸν ἑταίρου χώεται αἰνῶς
δείδω μὴ καὶ τεῖχος ὑπέρμορον ἐξαλαπάξῃ.
sentences.l:
but now, when indeed in heart for his companion he is incensed terribly,
I fear that even the wall, beyond fate, he may plunder utterly.”
sentences.i: but now that he is terribly incensed at heart for his companion, I fear that he may even plunder the wall, contrary to fate.”
sentences.n: χώεται is the present of χώομαι ‘be incensed’; θυμόν is an accusative of respect, ‘in heart’, and ἑταίρου ‘for his companion’ gives the cause (Patroclus is not named here). αἰνῶς is ‘terribly’. δείδω μή with the subjunctive means ‘I fear that’. τεῖχος ὑπέρμορον: ὑπέρμορον (ὑπέρ + μόρος ‘fate’) may be taken with the wall or as an adverb; either way the sense is ‘contrary to fate’, and the wall is evidently Troy’s. ἐξαλαπάξῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ἐξαλαπάζω ‘plunder utterly’. Zeus’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατο Κρονίδης, πόλεμον δ’ ἀλίαστον ἔγειρε.
sentences.l: So spoke the son of Cronus, and war, relentless, he was rousing.
sentences.i: So spoke the son of Cronus, and he was rousing relentless war.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατο ‘so he spoke’ is the stock close of a speech. Κρονίδης ‘son of Cronus’ is Zeus. ἀλίαστον ‘relentless’ is probably ἀ- + λιάζομαι ‘bend aside’, ‘not to be turned aside’. ἔγειρε is the unaugmented imperfect of ἐγείρω ‘rouse’.

sentences.t: βὰν δ’ ἴμεναι πόλεμον δὲ θεοὶ δίχα θυμὸν ἔχοντες·
sentences.l: And they set out to go to the war, the gods, with their hearts divided:
sentences.i: The gods set out for the war with their hearts divided:
sentences.n: βὰν is the unaugmented third plural aorist of βαίνω ‘go’ (Attic ἔβησαν), and ἴμεναι the epic infinitive of εἶμι ‘go’, so βὰν … ἴμεναι is ‘set out to go’. πόλεμον δέ ‘to the war’ has the suffix -δε of direction. δίχα θυμὸν ἔχοντες is ‘having their hearts apart’, that is, of two minds; the next lines show them splitting into two camps.

sentences.t:
Ἥρη μὲν μετ’ ἀγῶνα νεῶν καὶ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη
ἠδὲ Ποσειδάων γαιήοχος ἠδ’ ἐριούνης
Ἑρμείας, ὃς ἐπὶ φρεσὶ πευκαλίμῃσι κέκασται·
sentences.i: Hera went to the gathering of the ships, and Pallas Athena, and Poseidon, the earth-holder, and Hermes the helper, who excels in keen wits;
sentences.n: These are the gods who side with the Achaeans, though the Greek does not say so. μετ’ ἀγῶνα νεῶν is ‘to the gathering of the ships’: ἀγών is a gathering place, here where the ships are drawn up. γαιήοχος ‘earth-holder’ is Poseidon’s second epithet. Ἑρμείας is the Ionic form of Hermes; ἐριούνης is a stock epithet whose meaning is not known (‘helper’ is only an ancient guess), and the line break separates it from the name. ἐπὶ φρεσὶ πευκαλίμῃσι κέκασται is ‘excels in keen wits’: κέκασται is the perfect of καίνυμαι ‘excel’, and πευκαλίμος ‘keen’ is the traditional sense, its formation uncertain.

sentences.t:
Ἥφαιστος δ’ ἅμα τοῖσι κίε σθένεϊ βλεμεαίνων
χωλεύων, ὑπὸ δὲ κνῆμαι ῥώοντο ἀραιαί.
sentences.l:
And Hephaestus with them went, in his strength exulting,
limping, and beneath him his shanks moved nimbly, thin.
sentences.i: Hephaestus went with them, exulting in his strength, limping, his thin shanks moving nimbly beneath him.
sentences.n: κίε is the unaugmented imperfect of κίω ‘go’. σθένεϊ βλεμεαίνων ‘exulting in his strength’ is set beside χωλεύων ‘limping’ without comment; βλεμεαίνω ‘exult’ is the traditional sense and not certain. ὑπὸ δέ ‘beneath him’; κνῆμαι are the ‘shanks’, the lower legs, ῥώοντο the imperfect of ῥώομαι ‘move quickly, nimbly’, and ἀραιαί ‘thin’.

sentences.t:
ἐς δὲ Τρῶας Ἄρης κορυθαίολος, αὐτὰρ ἅμ’ αὐτῷ
Φοῖβος ἀκερσεκόμης ἠδ’ Ἄρτεμις ἰοχέαιρα
Λητώ τε Ξάνθός τε φιλομειδής τ’ Ἀφροδίτη.
sentences.l:
And to the Trojans Ares of the glancing helmet, and with him
Phoebus, with unshorn hair, and Artemis, the arrow-pourer,
and Leto and Xanthus and smile-loving Aphrodite.
sentences.i: Ares of the glancing helmet went to the Trojans, and with him Phoebus with unshorn hair, and Artemis, who showers her arrows, and Leto and Xanthus and smile-loving Aphrodite.
sentences.n: These are the gods on the Trojan side. κορυθαίολος is ‘of the glancing helmet’ (κόρυς ‘helmet’ + αἰόλος ‘quick-moving, glancing’). ἀκερσεκόμης is ‘with unshorn hair’ (ἀ- ‘not’, κείρω ‘cut’, κόμη ‘hair’). ἰοχέαιρα is ‘who showers her arrows’, its second element disputed (χέω ‘pour’ or χαίρω ‘delight in’). Xanthus is the river of the plain, and line 74 gives Xanthus as the gods’ name for it. Line 40 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the edition prints φιλομειδής with one μ, so the λο stands where the fourth foot needs a long syllable, and the doubled-μ form φιλομμειδής would scan; in Ἀφροδίτη the syllable before φρ stays short, as often in Homer.

sentences.t:
εἷος μέν ῥ’ ἀπάνευθε θεοὶ θνητῶν ἔσαν ἀνδρῶν,
τεῖος Ἀχαιοὶ μὲν μέγα κύδανον, οὕνεκ’ Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἐξεφάνη, δηρὸν δὲ μάχης ἐπέπαυτ’ ἀλεγεινῆς·
sentences.i: As long as the gods kept apart from mortal men, so long the Achaeans exulted greatly, because Achilles had appeared, after long ceasing from grievous fighting;
sentences.n: εἷος … τεῖος is the epic ‘as long as … so long’ (Attic ἕως … τέως). ἀπάνευθε ‘apart from’, with the genitive; ἔσαν is the third plural imperfect of εἰμί. κύδανον is the imperfect of κυδάνω ‘exult’ (from κῦδος ‘glory’). οὕνεκ’ is ‘because’. ἐξεφάνη is the aorist passive of ἐκφαίνω, ‘showed himself, appeared’, and ἐπέπαυτ’ the pluperfect middle of παύω, ‘had ceased’, with the genitive μάχης ἀλεγεινῆς ‘from grievous fighting’. The words from οὕνεκ’ to the end repeat words of an earlier part and keep its English.

sentences.t:
Τρῶας δὲ τρόμος αἰνὸς ὑπήλυθε γυῖα ἕκαστον
δειδιότας, ὅθ’ ὁρῶντο ποδώκεα Πηλεΐωνα
τεύχεσι λαμπόμενον βροτολοιγῷ ἶσον Ἄρηϊ.
sentences.l:
but upon the Trojans a fearsome trembling crept, upon the limbs of each,
being afraid, when they saw the fleet-footed son of Peleus
gleaming in his armour, equal to mortal-ruining Ares.
sentences.i: But a fearsome trembling crept over the limbs of every Trojan, in their fear, when they saw the fleet-footed son of Peleus gleaming in his armour, the equal of Ares, the ruin of mortals.
sentences.n: τρόμος αἰνός ‘fearsome trembling’; ὑπήλυθε is the aorist of ὑπέρχομαι ‘come over, creep over’; γυῖα ἕκαστον ‘the limbs of each’, with the singular ἕκαστον. δειδιότας is the perfect participle of δείδω ‘fear’, accusative plural agreeing with Τρῶας. ὁρῶντο is a middle form of ὁράω, ‘they saw’. λαμπόμενον τεύχεσι ‘gleaming in armour’ (τεύχεσι, dative plural of τεῦχος). βροτολοιγῷ ἶσον Ἄρηϊ is ‘equal to Ares, the ruin of mortals’ (βροτός + λοιγός ‘ruin’), a stock phrase, translated every time. The first line repeats words of an earlier part and keeps its English.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ μεθ’ ὅμιλον Ὀλύμπιοι ἤλυθον ἀνδρῶν,
ὦρτο δ’ Ἔρις κρατερὴ λαοσσόος, αὖε δ’ Ἀθήνη
στᾶσ’ ὁτὲ μὲν παρὰ τάφρον ὀρυκτὴν τείχεος ἐκτός,
ἄλλοτ’ ἐπ’ ἀκτάων ἐριδούπων μακρὸν ἀΰτει.
sentences.l:
But when into the throng of men the Olympians came,
up rose Strife, strong, rouser of the people, and Athena cried out,
standing now beside the dug ditch, outside the wall,
and at another time on the loud-echoing shores she shouted loudly.
sentences.i: But when the Olympians had come into the throng of men, strong Strife, rouser of the people, rose up, and Athena cried out, standing now beside the dug ditch outside the wall and now on the loud-echoing shores, shouting loudly.
sentences.n: Ὀλύμπιοι ‘the Olympians’ are the gods. ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rise’. Ἔρις ‘Strife’ is a person here, and κρατερή ‘strong’ and λαοσσόος ‘rouser of the people’ go with her (derivation disputed: ‘setting the people moving’ or ‘saving the people’). αὖε is the imperfect of ἀΰω ‘cry out’ and ἀΰτει the present of ἀΰτέω ‘shout’; the subject of both is Athena. στᾶσ’ is the aorist participle of ἵστημι, ‘having taken her stand’; ὁτὲ μέν … ἄλλοτε is ‘now … at another time’. τάφρον ὀρυκτήν ‘the dug ditch’ and τείχεος ἐκτός ‘outside the wall’. ἀκτάων ἐριδούπων ‘loud-echoing shores’; μακρόν is ‘loudly’, an adverb.

sentences.t:
αὖε δ’ Ἄρης ἑτέρωθεν ἐρεμνῇ λαίλαπι ἶσος
ὀξὺ κατ’ ἀκροτάτης πόλιος Τρώεσσι κελεύων,
ἄλλοτε πὰρ Σιμόεντι θέων ἐπὶ Καλλικολώνῃ.
sentences.l:
And Ares cried out from the other side, like a dusky squall,
shrilly, down from the topmost part of the city, bidding the Trojans on,
at another time beside the Simois running over Callicolone.
sentences.i: From the other side Ares cried out, like a dusky squall, calling on the Trojans shrilly from the very top of the city, and at another time running beside the Simois on Callicolone.
sentences.n: ἑτέρωθεν ‘from the other side’ is the Trojan side, answering Athena’s. ἐρεμνῇ λαίλαπι ἶσος is ‘like a dusky squall’ (λαῖλαψ ‘squall’, ἐρεμνός ‘dusky’). ὀξύ, literally ‘sharp’, is adverbial: ‘shrilly’. κατ’ ἀκροτάτης πόλιος is ‘down from the topmost part of the city’, with κατά and the genitive and -ιος for -εως. θέων is ‘running’. Σιμόεις is the Simois, a river by Troy; Καλλικολώνη is a place-name, in Greek ‘fair hill’, and ἐπί puts Ares on or over it.

sentences.t:
ὣς τοὺς ἀμφοτέρους μάκαρες θεοὶ ὀτρύνοντες
σύμβαλον, ἐν δ’ αὐτοῖς ἔριδα ῥήγνυντο βαρεῖαν·
sentences.l:
So the blessed gods, urging on both,
threw them together, and among them they burst out heavy strife;
sentences.i: So the blessed gods, urging on both sides, drove them together, and heavy strife broke out among them;
sentences.n: τοὺς ἀμφοτέρους ‘both’ are the two armies; ὀτρύνοντες ‘urging on’; σύμβαλον is the unaugmented aorist of συμβάλλω, ‘threw together’. ἔριδα ῥήγνυντο βαρεῖαν is ‘they burst out heavy strife’: ῥήγνυντο is the middle of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’, with ἔριδα as object. Whether ἐν δ’ αὐτοῖς ‘among them’ means the armies or the gods themselves the Greek leaves open, and the next lines show the gods striving too. μάκαρες θεοί ‘blessed gods’ is a stock phrase.

sentences.t:
δεινὸν δὲ βρόντησε πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε
ὑψόθεν·
sentences.l:
And dreadfully thundered the father of men and of gods
from on high;
sentences.i: And the father of men and of gods thundered dreadfully from on high;
sentences.n: δεινόν is the neuter used as an adverb, ‘dreadfully’, and βρόντησε the aorist of βροντάω ‘thunder’. πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε ‘father of men and of gods’ is Zeus, a stock phrase translated every time. ὑψόθεν ‘from on high’ is set against νέρθε in the next unit.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ νέρθε Ποσειδάων ἐτίναξε
γαῖαν ἀπειρεσίην ὀρέων τ’ αἰπεινὰ κάρηνα.
sentences.l:
and from below Poseidon shook
the earth, boundless, and the steep peaks of the mountains.
sentences.i: and from below Poseidon shook the boundless earth and the steep peaks of the mountains.
sentences.n: νέρθε ‘from below’ answers ὑψόθεν: the sky-god thunders and the sea-god shakes the ground. ἐτίναξε is the aorist of τινάσσω ‘shake’. ἀπειρεσίην is ‘boundless’. ὀρέων is the uncontracted genitive plural of ὄρος ‘mountain’, and κάρηνα, literally ‘heads’, is ‘peaks’.

sentences.t:
πάντες δ’ ἐσσείοντο πόδες πολυπίδακος Ἴδης
καὶ κορυφαί, Τρώων τε πόλις καὶ νῆες Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
And all were shaken, the feet of many-springed Ida
and its summits, and the city of the Trojans and the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: All of it shook: the foothills of many-springed Ida and its summits, the city of the Trojans and the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: ἐσσείοντο is the imperfect passive of σείω ‘shake’, with the doubled σ. πόδες, ‘feet’, of a mountain are its foothills. Ἴδης is Ida, the mountain by Troy, and πολυπίδακος ‘many-springed’ (πίδαξ ‘spring’) is its stock epithet. κορυφαί are ‘summits’. The earthquake takes in the city and the Achaean ships alike.

sentences.t:
ἔδεισεν δ’ ὑπένερθεν ἄναξ ἐνέρων Ἀϊδωνεύς,
δείσας δ’ ἐκ θρόνου ἆλτο καὶ ἴαχε,
sentences.l:
And he was afraid, beneath, the lord of the dead, Aidoneus,
and, afraid, leapt from his throne and cried out,
sentences.i: Beneath, Aidoneus, lord of the dead, was afraid, and in his fear leapt from his throne and cried out,
sentences.n: ὑπένερθεν ‘beneath’ and ἄναξ ἐνέρων: ἔνεροι are ‘those below’, the dead, so ‘lord of the dead’. Ἀϊδωνεύς ‘Aidoneus’ is another name for Hades. ἆλτο is the aorist middle of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’, and ἴαχε the aorist of ἰάχω ‘cry out’. The sentence runs on into the fear itself.

sentences.t:
μή οἱ ὕπερθε
γαῖαν ἀναρρήξειε Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων,
οἰκία δὲ θνητοῖσι καὶ ἀθανάτοισι φανείη
σμερδαλέ’ εὐρώεντα, τά τε στυγέουσι θεοί περ·
sentences.l:
lest above him
the earth Poseidon the earth-shaker should break open,
and to mortals and immortals the dwellings should appear
frightful, dank, which even the gods hate;
sentences.i: lest Poseidon the earth-shaker split the earth open above him, and the frightful, dank dwellings, which even the gods hate, be exposed to mortals and immortals;
sentences.n: μή with the optative gives a fear after a past verb: ‘lest he break’. ἀναρρήξειε is the aorist optative of ἀναρρήγνυμι ‘break open’, with γαῖαν as object and οἱ ὕπερθε ‘above him’. φανείη is the aorist passive optative of φαίνομαι, ‘should appear’, with the datives θνητοῖσι καὶ ἀθανάτοισι ‘to mortals and immortals’. οἰκία ‘dwellings’ are the house of the dead. σμερδαλέα ‘frightful’, εὐρώεντα ‘dank’; τά τε στυγέουσι θεοί περ is ‘which even the gods hate’.

sentences.t: τόσσος ἄρα κτύπος ὦρτο θεῶν ἔριδι ξυνιόντων.
sentences.l: So great a din arose, as the gods in strife came together.
sentences.i: Such was the din that arose as the gods came together in strife.
sentences.n: τόσσος is τόσος ‘so great’, with the doubled σ, and κτύπος is ‘din’, a crash or beating sound. ὦρτο ‘arose’. ξυνιόντων is a genitive plural participle of ξύνειμι (ξύν + εἶμι) ‘come together’, agreeing with θεῶν, and ἔριδι is ‘in strife’. The line sums up the thunder, the quake and the cry of Aidoneus.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι μὲν γὰρ ἔναντα Ποσειδάωνος ἄνακτος
ἵστατ’ Ἀπόλλων Φοῖβος ἔχων ἰὰ πτερόεντα,
ἄντα δ’ Ἐνυαλίοιο θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.i: For opposite Poseidon the lord stood Phoebus Apollo with his winged arrows, and opposite Enyalius stood the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena;
sentences.n: Now the gods are matched in pairs. ἤτοι μὲν γάρ ‘for indeed’ explains the din. ἔναντα and ἄντα both mean ‘opposite’ with the genitive, and ἵστατ’ is the unaugmented imperfect ‘stood’. ἰά ‘arrows’ is a plural of ἰός, and πτερόεντα ‘winged’. Ἐνυάλιος ‘Enyalius’ is a name of the war-god. θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη ‘the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena’ is a stock phrase.

sentences.t:
Ἥρῃ δ’ ἀντέστη χρυσηλάκατος κελαδεινὴ
Ἄρτεμις ἰοχέαιρα κασιγνήτη ἑκάτοιο·
sentences.l:
And against Hera stood the one of the golden distaff, the resounding,
Artemis, the arrow-pourer, sister of the far-darter;
sentences.i: And against Hera stood Artemis, who showers her arrows, she of the golden distaff, the resounding one, sister of the far-darter;
sentences.n: ἀντέστη is the aorist of ἀνθίστημι ‘stand against’, with the dative. χρυσηλάκατος is ‘of the golden distaff’ (ἠλακάτη ‘distaff’), and κελαδεινή ‘the resounding’, the sound not being said. ἑκάτοιο is ‘of the far-darter’, that is Apollo: ἕκατος is the short form behind ἑκατηβόλος, but the sense of the short form alone is not certain.

sentences.t:
Λητοῖ δ’ ἀντέστη σῶκος ἐριούνιος Ἑρμῆς,
ἄντα δ’ ἄρ’ Ἡφαίστοιο μέγας ποταμὸς βαθυδίνης,
ὃν Ξάνθον καλέουσι θεοί, ἄνδρες δὲ Σκάμανδρον.
sentences.l:
And against Leto stood the sturdy helper Hermes,
and opposite Hephaestus the great river, deep-eddying,
whom the gods call Xanthus, and men Scamander.
sentences.i: And against Leto stood Hermes the sturdy helper, and opposite Hephaestus the great river, deep-eddying, whom the gods call Xanthus, and men Scamander.
sentences.n: Λητοῖ is the dative of Λητώ. σῶκος is a stock epithet of Hermes whose meaning is not known; ‘sturdy’ is the traditional gloss and a guess. ἐριούνιος ‘helper’ is the same epithet as ἐριούνης in line 34, in another form, its meaning likewise not known. μέγας ποταμὸς βαθυδίνης is ‘the great river, deep-eddying’; it is the Xanthus of line 40. The last line says the river has two names, one used by gods and one by men.

sentences.t: ὣς οἳ μὲν θεοὶ ἄντα θεῶν ἴσαν·
sentences.l: So they, the gods, went opposite the gods;
sentences.i: So the gods went against the gods;
sentences.n: ὣς οἳ μέν ‘so they’ closes the pairings of the gods. ἴσαν is the third plural imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’, and ἄντα θεῶν ‘opposite the gods’ takes the genitive. With αὐτάρ the poem turns to the men.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς
Ἕκτορος ἄντα μάλιστα λιλαίετο δῦναι ὅμιλον
Πριαμίδεω·
sentences.i: But Achilles longed above all to plunge into the throng and meet Hector, son of Priam;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ turns from the gods to the men. Ἕκτορος ἄντα is ‘opposite Hector’ (ἄντα with the genitive). λιλαίετο is the imperfect of λιλαίομαι ‘long for’, with the infinitive δῦναι, the aorist of δύω ‘enter, plunge into’, and ὅμιλον ‘the throng’. Πριαμίδεω is the epic genitive of Πριαμίδης ‘son of Priam’, which agrees with Ἕκτορος.

sentences.t:
τοῦ γάρ ῥα μάλιστά ἑ θυμὸς ἀνώγει
αἵματος ἆσαι Ἄρηα ταλαύρινον πολεμιστήν.
sentences.l:
for of him most of all his heart bade him
to glut with blood Ares, the shield-enduring warrior.
sentences.i: for his heart bade him above all to glut Ares, the warrior who bears the hide shield, with that man’s blood.
sentences.n: τοῦ goes with αἵματος in the next line: ‘of his blood’, Hector’s, with the two words separated. ῥα is a light particle; μάλιστά ἑ θυμὸς ἀνώγει is ‘his heart bade him most of all’, ἑ being ‘him’ and ἀνώγει the pluperfect of ἄνωγα used as a past tense, ‘bade’. ἆσαι is the aorist infinitive of ἄω ‘satiate, glut’. Ἄρηα ‘Ares’ stands for the war-god and for war; ταλαύρινον ‘shield-enduring’ is the traditional sense (τλάω ‘endure’ + ῥινός ‘hide’), πολεμιστήν ‘warrior’. The last line repeats one in an earlier part and keeps its English.

sentences.t:
Αἰνείαν δ’ ἰθὺς λαοσσόος ὦρσεν Ἀπόλλων
ἀντία Πηλεΐωνος, ἐνῆκε δέ οἱ μένος ἠΰ·
sentences.l:
But Aeneas straight the rouser of the people Apollo roused
against the son of Peleus, and put into him good might;
sentences.i: But Apollo, rouser of the people, roused Aeneas straight against the son of Peleus and put good might into him;
sentences.n: Αἰνείαν is the object of ὦρσεν, the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’; ἰθύς is ‘straight’ and ἀντία Πηλεΐωνος ‘against the son of Peleus’. λαοσσόος ‘rouser of the people’ is the same epithet as Strife’s in line 48 (derivation disputed). ἐνῆκε is the aorist of ἐνίημι ‘put into’; μένος ἠΰ is ‘good might’, ἠΰ being the neuter of ἠΰς (= ἐΰς) ‘good’.

sentences.t: υἱέϊ δὲ Πριάμοιο Λυκάονι εἴσατο φωνήν·
sentences.l: and to the son of Priam, Lycaon, he made himself like in voice;
sentences.i: and he made himself like Lycaon, the son of Priam, in voice;
sentences.n: υἱέϊ Πριάμοιο Λυκάονι is a dative, ‘to the son of Priam, Lycaon’, the dative of likeness. εἴσατο is the aorist middle of εἴδομαι ‘make oneself like’ (‘seem’), and φωνήν an accusative of respect, ‘in voice’. Apollo is still the subject, and he takes only Lycaon’s voice.

sentences.t: τῷ μιν ἐεισάμενος προσέφη Διὸς υἱὸς Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.l: Having made himself like to that man, addressed him Zeus’ son Apollo:
sentences.i: Making himself like that man, Apollo, the son of Zeus, said to him:
sentences.n: ἐεισάμενος is the aorist participle of εἴδομαι with a doubled ε, ‘having made himself like’; τῷ ‘to that man’ is Lycaon and μιν ‘him’ is Aeneas. Διὸς υἱὸς Ἀπόλλων ‘Apollo, the son of Zeus’. The line is the same as one in an earlier part and has that unit’s English.

sentences.l:
“Aeneas, counsel-bearer of the Trojans, where are your threats
which to the kings of the Trojans you promised, drinking wine,
to fight head-on with Peleus’-son Achilles?”
sentences.i: “Aeneas, counsellor of the Trojans, where are your threats, those you promised the Trojan kings over your wine, to fight Peleus’ son Achilles head-on?”
sentences.n: Apollo speaks, in Lycaon’s voice. βουληφόρε is the vocative of βουληφόρος ‘counsel-bearer’ (βουλή + φέρω), ‘counsellor’. ἀπειλαί ‘threats’ are what Aeneas said he would do. ἃς … ὑπίσχεο is ‘which you promised’ (second singular imperfect of ὑπίσχομαι), and οἰνοποτάζων ‘drinking wine’ is a rare verb: the boasts were made over the cups. Πηλεΐδεω Ἀχιλῆος has the patronymic Πηλεΐδης ‘Peleus’ son’ with the epic genitive -εω. ἐναντίβιον ‘head-on’; πολεμίξειν is the future infinitive of πολεμίζω ‘fight’. Apollo’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Αἰνείας ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέειπε·
sentences.l: Him in turn Aeneas, answering, addressed:
sentences.i: In answer Aeneas said to him in turn:
sentences.n: This is the reply formula with a name in it. τόν ‘him’ is Apollo, whom Aeneas takes for Lycaon; αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘in turn’; ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ and προσέειπε ‘addressed’. The same formula with other names stands in the Odyssey.

sentences.t:
Πριαμίδη τί με ταῦτα καὶ οὐκ ἐθέλοντα κελεύεις
ἀντία Πηλεΐωνος ὑπερθύμοιο μάχεσθαι;
sentences.l:
“Priam’s-son, why me, these things, and unwilling, do you order
against the son of Peleus, the high-hearted, to fight?
sentences.i: “Son of Priam, why do you tell me, unwilling as I am, to fight against the high-hearted son of Peleus?
sentences.n: Aeneas answers. Πριαμίδη is a vocative, ‘son of Priam’: he thinks he is speaking to Lycaon. τί με ταῦτα κελεύεις is ‘why do you order me (to do) these things’, with καὶ οὐκ ἐθέλοντα ‘even unwilling’ agreeing with με. ἀντία + genitive is ‘against’, and μάχεσθαι is the infinitive after κελεύεις. ὑπερθύμοιο ‘high-hearted’ is ὑπέρ ‘over’ + θυμός ‘heart’, the genitive agreeing with Πηλεΐωνος; the Greek does not say whether it blames or praises.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γὰρ νῦν πρῶτα ποδώκεος ἄντ’ Ἀχιλῆος
στήσομαι, ἀλλ’ ἤδη με καὶ ἄλλοτε δουρὶ φόβησεν
ἐξ Ἴδης, ὅτε βουσὶν ἐπήλυθεν ἡμετέρῃσι,
πέρσε δὲ Λυρνησσὸν καὶ Πήδασον·
sentences.i: For this is not the first time I shall stand against fleet-footed Achilles; already once before he put me to flight with his spear from Ida, when he came upon our cattle, and sacked Lyrnessus and Pedasus;
sentences.n: νῦν πρῶτα is ‘now for the first time’. ἄντ’ is ἄντα ‘opposite’; στήσομαι is the future middle of ἵστημι ‘stand’. ἀλλ’ ἤδη … καὶ ἄλλοτε is ‘but already at another time’. φόβησεν is the aorist of φοβέω, ‘put to flight’, and δουρί the dative of δόρυ ‘spear’. ὅτε βουσὶν ἐπήλυθεν ἡμετέρῃσι is ‘when he came upon our cattle’ (βουσί, dative plural of βοῦς; ἡμετέρῃσι, epic feminine dative). πέρσε is the unaugmented aorist of πέρθω ‘sack’. Λυρνησσός and Πήδασος are place-names; the Greek does not say where they lie.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐμὲ Ζεὺς
εἰρύσαθ’, ὅς μοι ἐπῶρσε μένος λαιψηρά τε γοῦνα.
sentences.l:
but me Zeus
guarded, who roused in me might and swift knees.
sentences.i: but Zeus guarded me, he who roused might and swift knees in me.
sentences.n: εἰρύσαθ’ is the aorist middle of ἐρύομαι ‘guard, protect’ (εἰρύσατο, the last vowel elided). ὅς μοι ἐπῶρσε is ‘who roused in me’, the aorist of ἐπόρνυμι; the antecedent is Zeus. μένος ‘might’; λαιψηρά … γοῦνα ‘swift knees’, γοῦνα being the epic plural of γόνυ: the knees stand for the speed of the legs.

sentences.t:
ἦ κ’ ἐδάμην ὑπὸ χερσὶν Ἀχιλλῆος καὶ Ἀθήνης,
ἥ οἱ πρόσθεν ἰοῦσα τίθει φάος ἠδ’ ἐκέλευεν
ἔγχεϊ χαλκείῳ Λέλεγας καὶ Τρῶας ἐναίρειν.
sentences.l:
Truly I would have been subdued by the hands of Achilles and Athena,
who, going before him, was setting light for him and was ordering him
with bronze spear to slay Leleges and Trojans.
sentences.i: Truly I would have been overcome by the hands of Achilles and Athena, who went before him, set light for him, and told him to kill Leleges and Trojans with his bronze spear.
sentences.n: ἦ κ’ ἐδάμην is ‘I would truly have been’: ἦ (‘truly’) + κε + the aorist passive of δάμνημι ‘subdue, overcome’. ὑπὸ χερσίν ‘under the hands’. ἥ is the relative ‘who’, Athena; ἰοῦσα is the participle of εἶμι ‘go’. τίθει φάος ‘was setting light’: the line does not say what the light is; it may be a figure for a clear way or for the success Athena gave him, and the English keeps the Greek’s words. ἐκέλευεν ‘was ordering’; ἔγχεϊ χαλκείῳ ‘with a bronze spear’; ἐναίρειν ‘to slay’. Λέλεγες are the Leleges, a people named beside the Trojans.

sentences.t: τὼ οὐκ ἔστ’ Ἀχιλῆος ἐναντίον ἄνδρα μάχεσθαι·
sentences.l: Therefore it is not possible against Achilles for a man to fight;
sentences.i: That is why no man can fight against Achilles;
sentences.n: τώ is ‘therefore’. οὐκ ἔστ’ is ‘it is not possible’, with the infinitive μάχεσθαι and ἄνδρα as its accusative subject, ‘for a man to fight’. Ἀχιλῆος ἐναντίον ‘against Achilles’ takes the genitive.

sentences.t: αἰεὶ γὰρ πάρα εἷς γε θεῶν ὃς λοιγὸν ἀμύνει.
sentences.l: for always at hand is one at least of the gods, who wards off ruin.
sentences.i: for there is always at least one of the gods at his side to ward off ruin.
sentences.n: πάρα is πάρεστι ‘is at hand’, the preposition accented on its first syllable. εἷς γε θεῶν is ‘one at least of the gods’. ὃς λοιγὸν ἀμύνει is ‘who wards off ruin’; the ‘him’ it is warded off from is Achilles.

sentences.t:
καὶ δ’ ἄλλως τοῦ γ’ ἰθὺ βέλος πέτετ’, οὐδ’ ἀπολήγει
πρὶν χροὸς ἀνδρομέοιο διελθέμεν.
sentences.l:
And besides, of him at least straight flies the shaft, and does not stop
before through the flesh of a man to pass.
sentences.i: And besides, his shaft flies straight and never stops before it has passed through a man’s flesh.
sentences.n: καὶ δ’ ἄλλως is ‘and besides’ (ἄλλως ‘otherwise, in another respect’). τοῦ γ’ ‘his’ is Achilles’. ἰθύ is the adverb ‘straight’, πέτετ’ is πέτεται ‘flies’, and βέλος ‘shaft’ is the thrown spear. οὐδ’ ἀπολήγει ‘nor does it stop’; πρὶν … διελθέμεν is πρίν with the epic infinitive of διέρχομαι, ‘before passing through’; χροὸς ἀνδρομέοιο ‘a man’s flesh’ (ἀνδρόμεος ‘of a man’).

sentences.t:
εἰ δὲ θεός περ
ἶσον τείνειεν πολέμου τέλος, οὔ κε μάλα ῥέα
νικήσει’, οὐδ’ εἰ παγχάλκεος εὔχεται εἶναι.
sentences.l:
But if even a god stretched equal the end of war,
not at all easily would he win,
not even if all of bronze he claims to be.”
sentences.i: But if even a god were to stretch the outcome of the war out on equal terms, he would not win easily, not even if he claims to be all of bronze.”
sentences.n: εἰ … τείνειεν is εἰ with the optative, ‘if a god were to stretch’. ἶσον τείνειεν πολέμου τέλος is literally ‘stretch the end of war equal’: the picture of stretching or drawing out is not explained in the Greek, and the English keeps ‘stretch’ and says only that the god keeps the outcome level. νικήσει’ is νικήσειε with its last vowel elided, ‘would win’, and the unstated subject is Achilles. οὔ κε μάλα ῥέα is ‘not at all easily’; παγχάλκεος ‘all of bronze’; εὔχεται εἶναι ‘claims to be’. Aeneas’s speech ends here; the next part opens with Apollo’s reply.
